passage: Dilnaz waited until the other children left the counsellor's room. Her voice was small. "Baljeet Ma'am, an older cousin keeps trying to make me sit on his lap and touches me where I don't want. He says it's our secret." She stared at the carpet. "I told my aunt. She said I was imagining it." Baljeet Ma'am put down her pen and moved closer, but not too close. "Thank you for telling me. I believe you. It's not your fault, and it's not a secret you have to keep." She said she would call Dilnaz's mother and the school's safeguarding lead that same day, and she stayed with Dilnaz until they came.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz's aunt say when she first told her?
qa.a: She said Dilnaz was imagining it.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz stare at the carpet while speaking?
qa.a: She was probably scared and ashamed, and unsure if she would be believed again.

qa.q: What did Baljeet Ma'am do that helped Dilnaz?
qa.a: She said she believed her, that it wasn't her fault and wasn't a secret to keep, then stayed with her and called her mother and the safeguarding lead that same day.

qa.q: What would change if Dilnaz had stopped after her aunt didn't believe her?
qa.a: She might have stayed unsafe and alone, which is why telling again until someone believes you matters. 🤍

grounding: It shows a child reporting unwanted touch and telling again until a trusted adult believes her.

passage:
"Dhruv, can we talk about something important?"
"Is it about homework?"
"No. It's about your body." Sabina sat next to him. "The parts your swimming shorts cover are private. No one should touch them or ask to see them, except a doctor with me there."
"Even family?"
"Even family. And if someone says, 'Keep this secret,' about touching?"
"I tell you."
"Yes. And who else could you tell?"
"Papa. My class teacher."
"And if I don't listen?"
Dhruv thought. "Tell someone else. Keep telling."
"Exactly."

qa.q: What did Sabina say about the parts swimming shorts cover?
qa.a: Sabina said they are private and no one should touch or ask to see them, except a doctor with Sabina there.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv ask "Even family?"
qa.a: He seemed surprised and wanted to check whether the rule applied to people he knows and trusts.

qa.q: What makes Sabina's talk a good way to teach body safety?
qa.a: Sabina uses simple words, lets Dhruv name his own trusted adults and teaches him to keep telling until someone listens.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's class teacher be affected by being on his list?
qa.a: The class teacher becomes one of Dhruv's safe people, so they would need to listen carefully if he ever came to them.

grounding: It shows an adult teaching a child body boundaries, naming trusted adults and telling until believed.

passage: I'm Deepika. Last year, when I was twelve, my friend Tarun stopped wanting to go to his tuition class. He always had an excuse. One evening he told me the tuition teacher had touched him in a way that felt wrong, and said nobody would believe him. My stomach turned over. I remembered what we'd learned in school: private parts are private, and you tell a trusted adult. I said, "I believe you. Let's tell my mother together." We did. My mother listened, then helped his parents go to the school and the police. Tarun doesn't go there anymore. He still says I helped him most by believing him.

qa.q: What did Tarun say the tuition teacher told him?
qa.a: The teacher said nobody would believe him.

qa.q: What does Deepika's stomach turning over show?
qa.a: It shows Deepika was shocked and upset hearing what happened to a friend.

qa.q: What did Deepika do that helped Tarun?
qa.a: Deepika believed Tarun and went with him to tell Deepika's mother, a trusted adult.

qa.q: How might Tarun feel about Deepika now?
qa.a: Tarun feels grateful, saying Deepika helped most by believing him.

grounding: A first-person account of a child believing a friend and helping report abuse to trusted adults.

passage: Counsellor's note, class four, after the body-safety session. At break Ramesh (9) waited until the room emptied. He said an older cousin had been asking him to play a 'secret game' and touched him where his swimsuit covers. Ramesh told him no and went away. He told his mother, but she said, 'Don't make up stories about family.' He said, 'You told us to keep telling until someone believes.' I told him I believed him, that it was not his fault and that he did right to keep telling. I did not ask for details. I informed the principal the same day and followed our school's safeguarding steps, including a call with his father. I will check on Ramesh tomorrow. — Jatin Sir

qa.q: What did Ramesh's mother say when he first told her?
qa.a: She said, 'Don't make up stories about family.'

qa.q: What does Ramesh waiting until the room was empty suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He was probably scared and embarrassed and needed privacy, but he was determined to be heard.

qa.q: What did Jatin Sir do that was right?
qa.a: He believed Ramesh, told him it wasn't his fault, did not push for details and followed the school's safety steps the same day.

qa.q: How might it feel for Ramesh to hear 'I believe you' after not being believed at home?
qa.a: It would likely bring huge relief and help him trust that telling was worth it. 🤍

grounding: Shows a child who said no to unsafe touch and kept telling trusted adults until he was believed.

passage: Thursday. Today in school we learned the swimsuit rule: nobody can touch the parts a swimsuit covers, and nobody can ask you to keep secrets about touching. Ma'am said good secrets are like surprise parties; bad secrets make your tummy feel wrong. We traced our hands and wrote one trusted adult on each finger. Mine: Mummy, Papa, Baljeet mama, Class Ma'am, and Dadi. Ma'am said if one person doesn't listen, tell the next finger, and the next. I thought about the time Chachi kept squeezing my cheeks and I hated it. Mummy said I'm allowed to say 'no thank you'. I stuck the hand picture on my cupboard. — Lokesh

qa.q: How many trusted adults did Lokesh write on the traced hand?
qa.a: Five: Mummy, Papa, Baljeet mama, Class Ma'am and Dadi.

qa.q: What might Lokesh have been feeling on remembering Chachi squeezing Lokesh's cheeks?
qa.a: Lokesh remembered hating it and was likely relieved to know it is okay to say no to touch that feels unwanted.

qa.q: Why is the 'tell the next finger' idea helpful for children?
qa.a: It shows that if one adult doesn't listen, they should keep telling others until someone helps.

qa.q: How might Lokesh's parents feel seeing the hand picture on the cupboard?
qa.a: They might feel glad Lokesh knows the rules and that they are among the trusted adults on the list.

grounding: A child records learning body-boundary rules and naming trusted adults to tell.

passage:
In the village school near Aizawl, Ms Lalremsiami drew a simple outline on the board.
“The parts covered by your swimsuit are private,” she said. “No one may touch them, or ask you to keep a secret about them. Not a stranger, not someone you know.”
Chandrika, ten, put up her hand. “What if we tell someone and they don't listen?”
“Then you tell someone else. And someone else. Until someone believes you.”
Each child wrote three trusted adults on a card. Chandrika wrote: Ma, Ms Lalremsiami, my Aunty Sanga.
She folded the card and kept it in her pencil box.

qa.q: How many trusted adults did each child write down?
qa.a: Three trusted adults.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel about the question she asked?
qa.a: She felt a little worried about not being believed, and reassured by the teacher's answer.

qa.q: What did Ms Lalremsiami teach that is important?
qa.a: That no one may touch private parts, and to keep telling trusted adults until someone believes you.

qa.q: How might the other children feel after the lesson?
qa.a: They may feel safer, knowing their bodies belong to them and whom to tell.

grounding: A teacher teaches ten-year-olds about body boundaries, trusted adults and telling until believed.

passage:
After school in Lagos, Yara, nine, lingered by Mr Emeka's desk until the others left.
“Sir… Uncle Tunde next door made me sit on his lap and touched me where it's private. He said it's our secret.”
Mr Emeka stayed very calm and put down his pen. “Thank you for telling me, Yara. You were brave. It is not your fault.”
He didn't leave her alone. He asked a colleague to fetch the head of safeguarding, Mrs Adeyemi, while he sat with Yara. Mrs Adeyemi came at once, listened, and called Yara's mother that afternoon. Together they made a plan so Yara would not go next door again.

qa.q: Who did Mr Emeka ask a colleague to fetch?
qa.a: The head of safeguarding, Mrs Adeyemi.

qa.q: How was Yara feeling when she lingered by the desk?
qa.a: She felt scared and uneasy, carrying a secret she knew was wrong.

qa.q: What did Mr Emeka do that made him a safe adult?
qa.a: He stayed calm, thanked her, told her it was not her fault, stayed with her and got the safeguarding lead the same day.

qa.q: How might Yara's mother feel when Mrs Adeyemi calls?
qa.a: She would likely be shocked and upset, but grateful Yara told a trusted adult.

grounding: A nine-year-old tells her teacher about unsafe touch, and the school responds the same day.

passage:
At break, Omkar, eleven, found his friend Nikhil sitting alone on the stairs.
“What's wrong?”
Nikhil twisted his fingers. “The tuition sir plays a secret game. He touches me. He says don't tell or I'll fail.”
Omkar felt his stomach drop. “That's not okay. That's not a game.”
“Don't tell anyone!”
“We have to. It's not your fault. Come with me.”
Omkar walked Nikhil straight to Ms Uma, the counsellor. She listened calmly, told Nikhil he was brave and not to blame, and called his parents while both boys sat in her room. She said she would report it that same day.

qa.q: What did the tuition sir say would happen if Nikhil told?
qa.a: He said Nikhil would fail.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when Nikhil told him?
qa.a: He felt shocked and worried, his stomach dropping.

qa.q: Why was going to Ms Uma the right step?
qa.a: It got a trusted adult involved immediately who could protect Nikhil and report the abuse.

qa.q: How might Nikhil feel after Ms Uma responds?
qa.a: He may feel frightened but relieved and safer, knowing he is believed.

grounding: An eleven-year-old helps a friend tell a counsellor about abuse, and she acts the same day.

passage:
I'm Pooja. Varun sits next to me. For two weeks he's been saying he doesn't want to go to his extra swimming lesson. He picks at his nails and goes quiet when anyone says "swimming".
Today at break I asked him why. He looked around and whispered that the coach says it's their secret and touches him where his swimsuit covers. He said, "Don't tell."
I said, "This isn't a secret you should keep." I went with him straight to our class teacher.
She listened, told Varun it was not his fault, and took us both to the principal's office. The principal called Varun's parents right away and said the coach would not see any students.

qa.q: Where does Varun say the coach touches him?
qa.a: Where his swimsuit covers.

qa.q: What does Varun picking at his nails suggest?
qa.a: Varun seems anxious and upset about the swimming lessons.

qa.q: What did Pooja do that was right?

qa.a: Varun would stay alone with the problem and could keep being harmed, because no adult would know to protect him.

grounding: A classmate helps a boy report unsafe touch to a teacher, who acts the same day.

passage:
Sabina, you asked why I made you learn the names of your trusted adults. Let me tell you why.
When I was about your age, a man who ran the paan shop near our house used to call me in for sweets. One day he tried to touch me where my swimsuit would cover. I pushed his hand away and ran.
I was so scared I didn't want to tell. But I told my mother that same evening. She held me and said, "You did right. It's not your fault." That night she and my father went to the elders, and the shop was shut.
I was lucky: she believed me the first time. If she hadn't, I should have told someone else, and kept telling. That's what your Farida nani wants you to know.

qa.q: What did the man at the paan shop use to call Farida in for?
qa.a: Sweets.

qa.q: What was young Farida feeling when she didn't want to tell?
qa.a: Farida felt scared and perhaps ashamed, even though it wasn't her fault.

qa.q: What choice did young Farida make that evening, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She told her mother that same evening, which let an adult protect her and stop the man.

qa.q: How might Farida's mother have felt when Farida told her?
qa.a: Her mother was likely shocked and angry at the man but deeply protective of Farida, which is why she acted that night.

grounding: A grandmother tells her granddaughter how she reported unsafe touch as a child and was protected.

passage:
On the second night of school camp, a helper told Minakshi to come to the store room alone for a "special game" and tried to touch her under her swimsuit. She pulled away and ran out.
Her class teacher, the one she'd have told, was away sick. The phones were locked in the office. Minakshi was shaking. Her friend Jasleen said, "Who else is on your list? Ma'am said name three."
"The warden," Minakshi whispered.
They went straight to her room. The warden listened without interrupting, said, "You did right to tell me. This is not your fault," and kept Minakshi beside her. She called the camp head and Minakshi's parents that night, and the helper was sent away before breakfast.

qa.q: Why couldn't Minakshi tell her class teacher?
qa.a: Her class teacher was away sick, and the phones were locked in the office.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling when she reached Jasleen?
qa.a: Minakshi was frightened and shaken, and whispered when she answered.

qa.q: Why did having a list of trusted adults help Minakshi?
qa.a: When the first adult was missing, she already knew the next person to go to, so she didn't have to stay silent.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel after going with Minakshi to the warden?
qa.a: Jasleen might feel shaken too, but relieved and glad she helped her friend reach someone who acted straight away. 🤍

grounding: Shows a child refusing unsafe touch and, when one trusted adult is away, telling the next one, who acts the same night.

passage:
Diwali evening in the Mumbai flat was full of relatives. A distant uncle kept pulling Shankar onto his lap and tickling him, even after Shankar squirmed and said "stop".
Shankar slipped into the kitchen where his mother, Rukmini, was frying puris. "Amma, I don't like how Uncle keeps grabbing me."
Rukmini turned off the stove. "Thank you for telling me. Your body is yours. You can say no, even to family." She walked out with him and said, calmly and loud enough, "Shankar doesn't want to be tickled. High-fives only, please."
The uncle laughed it off, but stopped. Later, on the balcony, Rukmini asked Shankar to name the grown-ups he could always tell. He counted on his fingers: Amma, Appa, his class teacher, Paati.

qa.q: Where was Rukmini when Shankar came to tell her?
qa.a: She was in the kitchen, frying puris.

qa.q: Why did Shankar slip into the kitchen?
qa.a: Shankar felt uncomfortable and uneasy because the uncle kept grabbing and tickling him even after he said "stop".

qa.q: Which of Rukmini's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: She turned off the stove to listen and then spoke up in front of the uncle, which showed Shankar that his "no" would be backed up.

qa.q: How might the uncle see Rukmini's words, even while laughing it off?
qa.a: He may have felt a bit embarrassed at being corrected in public, but he understood clearly enough to stop.

grounding: Illustrates a child saying no to unwanted touch from a relative and a parent backing him and naming trusted adults.

"Okay, Class 3, winter safety week," said Sunaina Ma'am. "Who can touch the parts your swimsuit covers?"

Gautam put his hand up. "A doctor, if Mummy or Papa is there and you know why."

passage:
The summer I was ten, I went to a craft camp. I'm Aadhya. An older boy who helped the teacher kept trying to make me sit on his lap, and once he touched me where no one is allowed to. He said, "It's our secret."
I remembered what our school counsellor said: private parts are private, secrets that feel bad are not secrets, and keep telling until someone listens.
That evening I told Madhuri Masi. She stopped chopping onions, sat right next to me and listened. She said, "Thank you for telling me. This is not your fault." She called Mumma and the camp director that same night. The director came to our house the next morning, and the boy was removed from the camp.
Masi stayed with me that night. I was scared, but not alone.

qa.q: What did the older boy say about what he did?
qa.a: He said, "It's our secret."

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling after telling Madhuri Masi?
qa.a: Aadhya was still scared but felt safer and not alone, because Masi believed and stayed with her.

qa.q: What did Madhuri Masi do right when Aadhya told her?
qa.a: She stopped what she was doing, listened, said it was not Aadhya's fault, and called Mumma and the camp director the same night.

qa.q: How might the camp director's quick response affect other children at the camp?
qa.a: Removing the boy protects other children too and shows them that adults take such reports seriously.

grounding: Shows a child knowing body boundaries, recognising a bad secret, and telling a trusted adult who acts the same day.
